author: muhammad-zaheer
description: Up to 50 metals, glass treated with potassium, cobalt from the Congo and lithium from Chile: a phone is the planet in concentrated form. And when it dies, its materials are still precious.

hero.hook: Your phone looks like a single object, but it hides dozens of materials dug out of the ground on several continents.

blocks.text: A smartphone looks like a single object. In fact it is an assembly of dozens of materials from all over the world, far beyond the visible glass, plastic and metal. According to the European Commission, a phone can contain up to **50 different metals**. The US Geological Survey estimates that at least half of the components in a mobile device come from minerals mined from the ground or processed from them.

Why does such a small object need so many different materials? Because each part demands a specific property: carrying electricity, staying transparent, behaving like a magnet or storing energy. In other words, much of your phone begins its life as rock dug from the ground.

The screen needs a cover that is both transparent and strong. Many phones use [[Gorilla Glass]], a toughened glass made of [[silicon]], aluminum and oxygen. Its strength comes from a clever treatment: near the surface, the small sodium atoms are replaced with larger potassium atoms. These bulkier ions crowd the surface and create a pressure that stops cracks from spreading.

Just beneath the cover there is often a thin layer of [[indium tin oxide]], a material with rare properties: it conducts electricity while staying transparent. When a finger touches the screen, it changes the electrical signal in this layer. The phone detects that change without hiding any of the image underneath.

sections.title: Even the glass has a job

blocks.text: Beneath the screen, every material has been chosen for a task. The tiny circuits etched into the chips are built on silicon. Copper carries electricity between the components. The battery relies on [[lithium]] and graphite, a form of carbon, to store and release energy.

blocks.caption: A smartphone's logic board: silicon chips, copper traces and gold-plated contacts.

blocks.text: Not gold, not lithium: the most abundant metal in a smartphone is **copper**, which links all the components together.

Tiny but very powerful magnets for the speakers, microphones and vibration motor are made from [[rare-earth elements]] such as neodymium. The phone also contains minute amounts of precious metals, gold and silver. **Gold** is especially useful: it conducts electricity well and does not corrode, which makes it ideal for the small, reliable electrical connections inside the device.

Your phone may carry a "made in..." label, but its materials rarely come from a single country. Before reaching the final factory, they have often crossed several continents. Most of the world's [[cobalt]], a key battery metal, is mined in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Lithium, for its part, is produced in countries such as Australia, Chile, China and Argentina.

blocks.caption: Lithium evaporation ponds in the Salar de Atacama, Chile.

blocks.text: These raw materials are then refined, and turned into components somewhere else, before the phone is assembled. A smartphone is therefore a truly global product, whose journey begins long before the factory. And that journey has a price: mining and refining need land, water and energy, all of which come with an environmental cost.

sections.title: A phone that has traveled the world

blocks.text: A phone becomes useless when it stops working and can no longer be repaired. But the materials inside it keep their value: they can be recovered and reused. In **2022**, the world produced **62 million metric tons** of [[electronic waste]], smartphones included. Barely more than **20%** of it was collected and recycled.

blocks.caption: Old mobile phones and electronic waste waiting to be recycled.

blocks.text: Recovering those materials reduces the need to mine and process new raw materials. It also keeps valuable resources in use for longer. A phone can grow old. The materials inside it do not. The whole challenge is to keep them in use for as long as possible.
A smartphone is a mine in your pocket, up to 50 metals from several continents, and the real challenge is not replacing it but keeping its materials in circulation for as long as possible.

sections.title: An old phone is still precious
